President Trump will hit the campaign trail
in the Midwest today.
He'll campaign on behalf of Republican candidates
in Iowa and Kansas.
NPR's Stephen Fowler reports.
The president is holding his final in-person rallies
of the midterms in two states he won decisively in 2024,
but now have a lot of voters unhappy with his agenda.
His first stop, Dubuque, Iowa,
in the second congressional district
that Trump won by double digits,
but now is on the edge of the competitive map.
Then Trump goes to Kansas where polls show
Republicans could take control of the governor's office,
but lose the Senate race
in another heavily conservative state.
Both parties are spending hundreds of millions of dollars
in these last few days to get out the vote
with a larger than usual number of House and Senate races
expected to be close.
Stephen Fowler, NPR News.
Iran's leaders say they will respond forcefully
to any attack on their country,
even as the Iranian foreign minister pushes for diplomacy.
NPR's Hadil El-Shalchi reports.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard course spokesman,
Hossein Muhabbi, told Iranian state media on Sunday
that there will be, quote, "no geographical limitations,"
end quote, during a possible war with the U.S. and Israel.
He said the directive came from Ayatollah Mushtaba Khamenei,
who on Saturday said any threat to Iran
would face a, quote, "immediate and impactful response."
Muhabbi said the Revolutionary Guard
has identified new targets for a potential war,
but did not provide details on what they were.
Meanwhile, during an interview with news network Al Jazeera,
Iran's foreign minister, Basarakji, said Iran reached
a new proposal with mediators to reopen
the Strait of Hormuz in two days.
He did not elaborate on the details.
Hadil El-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
The U.S. and Israel have signaled a potential return
to hostilities after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
A federal judge has dismissed President Trump's lawsuit
against the Wall Street Journal,
as NPR's Stephen Besaha reports.
The suit involved a birthday card Trump allegedly sent
to late convicted sex offender, Jeffrey Epstein.
- The letter included a drawing of a naked woman
and what appeared to be the president's signature.
The journal reported this in July last year.
Trump denied anything to do with the letter
and called the journal's story fake
and sued for at least $10 billion in damages.
The federal judge dismissed the lawsuit,
declining to rule on whether the actual reporting was false
and saying the president had failed to show
the journal had acted with actual malice.
This is the second time Trump has tried
to sue the Wall Street Journal over this reporting.
The latest case was dismissed with prejudice,
preventing Trump from filing another lawsuit.
Stephen Besaha, NPR News, Birmingham, Alabama.
- Binance says customers are now able to make withdrawals
from their system once again
with those withdrawals being done in phases.
In a post on X, Binance says 95% of an estimated $6 billion
in funds stolen by hackers is recovered.
You're listening to NPR.
How do people in the UK know Christmas is coming?
An annual tea towel.
Vicki Barker reports from London.
- Since 2018, Nicki Haslam, socialite, social arbiter
and interior designer to royals and the merely rich,
has produced a tea towel,
skewering the things he has deemed common that year.
2024's list included unpeeled tomatoes
and barn conversions.
2025's indicted air fryers and playing wordle.
Among the items for 2026, standup comedians,
posh dog food and beards.
Apparently the clean shaven Haslam does not think it common
to charge 50 pounds, about $67 for a tea towel
or about $80 if you want it signed.
For NPR News, I'm Vicki Barker in London.
An immigrant rights group says more than four
out of 10 names the Trump administration flagged
as possible non-citizen voters in California
are not even on the state's voter rolls.
An analysis by UCLA's Voting Rights Project
is the first outside analysis of the list
the Department of Justice is using as part of an effort
to challenge voters in Democratic California.
The analysis also found thousands of US citizens appear
on the Justice Department's list.
The administration has demanded California election officials
separate out more than 20,000 names on the voter rolls.
Multiple judges have rejected the demand
as unconstitutional.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.
